title: As long as, unless, in case
seoTitle: As long as, unless, in case in Turkish
intro: This unit adds the last converbs of B2: conditions that must keep holding (**as long as**), that must not hold (**unless**) or that might happen (**in case**), a family of time clauses (**the moment**, **just as**, **ever since**, **until**), and the paired words *hem … hem*, *ne … ne* and *ister … ister*. Almost everything is built on what you know: the `-DIk` participle with a possessive from [B1 unit 6](gp-participle-dik), and `-(y)An` from [B1 unit 5](gp-participle-an).

blocks.text: `-DIğI sürece` (literally **in the time that…**) sets a condition that has to keep holding: *Çalıştığın sürece başarırsın* (As long as you work at it, you'll succeed). The clause is the `-DIk` participle with a possessive for its subject, then *sürece*. A noun subject stays in the nominative: *Hava güzel olduğu sürece provayı bahçede yaparız* (As long as the weather's nice, we'll rehearse in the garden).

lines: çalış- + tığ + ın + sürece  →  çalıştığın sürece

rows.en: as long as he, she or it works
as long as you work (plural or polite)

blocks.title: *çalışmamak*: as long as I don't work…

rows.en: as long as I don't work
as long as you don't work
as long as he, she or it doesn't work
as long as we don't work
as long as you don't work (plural or polite)
as long as they don't work

blocks.text: There is no question form of the clause: the question goes on the main verb, *Burada kaldığın sürece bize yardım eder misin?* (Will you help us as long as you're staying here?).

**With nouns and adjectives**, use *olduğu sürece*: *Burada olduğum sürece* (as long as I'm here), *Sağlığımız yerinde olduğu sürece* (as long as we're in good health). *Var* becomes *olduğu*: *Vaktim olduğu sürece sana yardım ederim* (As long as I have time, I'll help you).

**The negative**, `-mAdIğI sürece`, means **as long as … not**, which is close to **unless**: *Sen istemediğin sürece kimseye söylemem* (As long as you don't want me to, I won't tell anyone). The next section gives a shorter way to say this.

**müddetçe.** `-DIğI müddetçe` means the same and sounds more formal or bookish: *Kurallara uyduğunuz müddetçe bir sorun olmaz* (As long as you follow the rules, there won't be a problem). *Müddet* is an old word for **period**.

items.tr: Her gün çalıştığın sürece bağlamayı öğrenirsin.
items.seg: Her gün çalış|tığ|ın sürece bağlama|y|ı öğren|ir|sin.
items.en: As long as you practise every day, you'll learn the bağlama.

items.tr: Vaktim olduğu sürece sana yardım ederim.
items.seg: Vakt|im ol|duğ|u sürece sana yardım ed|er|im.
items.en: As long as I have time, I'll help you.

items.tr: Hava güzel olduğu sürece provayı bahçede yapalım.
items.seg: Hava güzel ol|duğ|u sürece prova|y|ı bahçe|de yap|a|lım.
items.en: As long as the weather is nice, let's rehearse in the garden.

items.tr: Sen istemediğin sürece kimseye söylemem.
items.en: As long as you don't want me to, I won't tell anyone.

items.tr: Kurallara uyduğunuz müddetçe bir sorun olmaz.
items.seg: Kural|lar|a uy|duğ|unuz müddetçe bir sorun ol|maz.
items.en: As long as you follow the rules, there won't be a problem.

blocks.text: English **as long as** can also be a length of time: **Stay as long as you like** is *İstediğin kadar kal*, with *kadar*. *Sürece* always sets a condition.

You met `-DIkçA` (**the more**, **whenever**) in [B1 unit 8](gp-dikca). Its negative, `-mAdIkçA`, means **unless**, or **as long as … not**: *Çalışmadıkça ilerleyemezsin* (Unless you practise, you can't make progress). The main clause is usually negative too, and the pair says that one thing won't happen without the other.

Like `-DIkçA`, it takes **no possessive**: the subject is a separate word, in the nominative: *Sen söylemedikçe kimse bilmez* (Unless you tell, nobody will know), *Usta izin vermedikçe çırak sahneye çıkmaz* (Unless the master allows it, the apprentice doesn't go on stage). The D of `-DIk` follows the negative's vowel, so it is always d: *-madıkça*, *-medikçe*.

In everyday speech the plain negative conditional is the most common: *Davet edilmezsem gitmem* (If I'm not invited, I won't go). `-mAdIkçA` adds a firmer tone, like **not unless**: *Mecbur kalmadıkça gece araba kullanmam* (I don't drive at night unless I have to).

items.tr: Çalışmadıkça ilerleyemezsin.
items.en: Unless you practise, you can't make progress.

items.tr: Sen söylemedikçe kimse bilmez.
items.en: Unless you tell, nobody will know.

items.tr: Bilet almadıkça içeri giremezsiniz.
items.en: You can't go in unless you buy a ticket.

items.tr: Mecbur kalmadıkça gece araba kullanmam.
items.en: I don't drive at night unless I have to.

blocks.text: No possessive: *çalışmadıkça*, never *çalışmadığımca*. And don't mix it up with `-mAdAn` (without, before; [B1 unit 7](gp-madan)): *Bilet almadan girdi* (He went in without buying a ticket) tells what happened; *Bilet almadıkça giremez* (He can't go in unless he buys a ticket) sets a condition.

sections.title: Yağdığı takdirde: in case, in the event that

blocks.text: Three more ways to say **if** belong to rules, contracts, announcements and careful speech. They add weight rather than meaning.

head: Form
Example
Meaning
rows: In the event of rain, the concert will be postponed.
Yağmur yağması hâlinde konser salonda yapılacaktır.
In case of rain, the concert will take place in the hall.
Bir gün Kars'a gidecek olursan bana haber ver.
If you ever happen to go to Kars, let me know.

blocks.text: **-DIğI takdirde** (literally **in the estimate that…**) is the formal **if, in the event that**. It is built like `-DIğI sürece`, with the possessive for the subject: *Bileti kaybettiğiniz takdirde para iadesi yapılmaz* (If you lose your ticket, no refund will be given). The negative is `-mAdIğI takdirde`: *Ödeme yapılmadığı takdirde rezervasyonunuz iptal edilecektir* (If payment is not made, your booking will be cancelled).

**Hâlinde** (in the state of) follows a noun or the verbal noun `-mA` with a possessive ([B1 unit 4](gp-ma-possessive)): *yangın hâlinde* (in case of fire), *acil durum hâlinde* (in an emergency), *trenin gecikmesi hâlinde* (should the train be late). You read it on signs and in instructions: *Yangın hâlinde asansörü kullanmayınız*. TDK writes *hâl* with a circumflex; print often leaves it out.

**-(y)AcAk olursa** (if it should happen that) is the future participle plus the conditional of *olmak*. It is spoken as well as written, and it imagines something less likely or not yet planned: *Bir gün İstanbul'a gelecek olursan bize de uğra* (If you ever come to Istanbul, drop by and see us). The person goes on *olursa*. For a negative, the plain conditional is more usual: *gelmezsen*. [C1 unit 1](gp-acak-olsa) adds *gelecek olsa*.

rows.en: if he, she or it should come
if you should come (plural or polite)

items.tr: Bileti kaybettiğiniz takdirde para iadesi yapılmaz.
items.seg: Bilet|i kaybet|tiğ|iniz takdirde para iade|si yap|ıl|maz.
items.en: If you lose your ticket, no refund will be given.

items.tr: Yağmur yağması hâlinde konser salonda yapılacaktır.
items.seg: Yağmur yağ|ma|sı hâlinde konser salon|da yap|ıl|acak|tır.
items.en: In case of rain, the concert will take place in the hall.

items.tr: Yangın hâlinde asansörü kullanmayınız.
items.en: In case of fire, do not use the lift.

items.tr: Ödeme yapılmadığı takdirde rezervasyonunuz iptal edilecektir.
items.seg: Ödeme yap|ıl|ma|dığ|ı takdirde rezervasyon|unuz iptal ed|il|ecek|tir.
items.en: If payment is not made, your booking will be cancelled.

items.tr: Bir gün Kars'a gidecek olursan âşık kahvelerini mutlaka gör.
items.seg: Bir gün Kars'a gid|ecek ol|ur|sa|n âşık kahve|ler|i|n|i mutlaka gör.
items.en: If you ever go to Kars, be sure to see the minstrels' coffeehouses.

blocks.text: In conversation the plain conditional does all these jobs: *Yağmur yağarsa konser salonda olacak*. Use *takdirde* and *hâlinde* when you write rules, and recognize them when you read them.

sections.title: Geldiği an, geldiğinden beri: more time clauses

blocks.text: You can already say **when** with `-(y)IncA` and `-DIğIndA` ([B1 unit 7](gp-ince), [B1 unit 8](gp-diginda)). The `-DIk` participle with a possessive also stands before nouns of time, and that gives a whole family of time clauses.

head: Form
Example
Meaning
rows: Let me know when you come.
The moment the music started, everyone fell silent.
Just as she went on stage, the lights went out.
Buraya taşındığımızdan beri her hafta konsere gidiyoruz.
Ever since we moved here, we've gone to a concert every week.
We waited until the concert ended.

blocks.text: **-DIğI zaman** is the everyday twin of `-DIğIndA`: *Eve geldiğim zaman seni ararım* means the same as *Eve geldiğimde seni ararım*. **-DIğI an** (the moment) and **-DIğI sırada** (just as, while) narrow it down: *an* is a point in time, *sıra* a stretch: *Ben çıktığım sırada telefon çaldı* (Just as I was leaving, the phone rang).

**-DIğIndAn beri** (since) counts from a starting point. As with `-DAn beri` after a noun ([A2 unit 9](gp-duration-dir)), the main verb is usually in the present continuous: *Bağlama çalmaya başladığımdan beri her gün çalışıyorum* (Ever since I started playing the bağlama, I've practised every day). It answers *Ne zamandan beri?* The `-(y)AlI` of [B1 unit 7](gp-ali) says much the same: *Başlayalı her gün çalışıyorum*.

rows.en: since he, she or it started

blocks.text: **-(y)AnA kadar** (until) is the `-(y)An` participle in the dative, then *kadar*: *Sen gelene kadar bekleriz* (We'll wait until you come). It is the everyday form of `-(y)IncAyA kadar` ([B1 unit 7](gp-ince)), and like it, it takes no possessive: the subject is a separate word.

items.tr: Müzik başladığı an herkes sustu.
items.en: The moment the music started, everyone fell silent.

items.tr: Sahneye çıktığı sırada ışıklar söndü.
items.en: Just as she went on stage, the lights went out.

items.tr: Bağlama çalmaya başladığımdan beri her gün çalışıyorum.
items.seg: Bağlama çal|ma|y|a başla|dığ|ım|dan beri her gün çalış|ıyor|um.
items.en: Ever since I started playing the bağlama, I've practised every day.

items.tr: Konser bitene kadar kimse yerinden kalkmadı.
items.seg: Konser bit|en|e kadar kimse yer|i|n|den kalk|ma|dı.
items.en: Nobody got up from their seat until the concert ended.

items.tr: Annem geldiği zaman birlikte yeriz.
items.en: When my mother comes, we'll eat together.

blocks.text: Without *beri*, `-DIğIndAn` means **because** ([B1 unit 8](gp-digi-icin)): *Geç kaldığından otobüsü kaçırdı* (He missed the bus because he was late). Only *-DIğIndAn beri* is **since**: *Geldiğinden beri hiç konuşmadı* (He hasn't said a word since he came).

sections.title: Hem … hem, ne … ne: paired words

blocks.text: Like English **both … and** and **either … or**, Turkish puts a small word before each of two (or more) items.

head: Pair
Example
Meaning
rows: Hem şarkı söylüyor hem bağlama çalıyor.
She both sings and plays the bağlama.
I drink neither tea nor coffee.
Ya bu akşam ya yarın gelirim.
I'll come either tonight or tomorrow.
Come by bus or by train, whichever you like.
Gerek öğrenciler gerekse öğretmenler konsere katıldı.
Both students and teachers attended the concert.

blocks.text: **Hem … hem (de)** adds the second item to the first: *Hem güldük hem ağladık* (We laughed and cried). With two subjects the verb may be singular or plural: *Hem Ali hem Ayşe geldi* or *geldiler*. *Hem de* on its own you met in [B2 unit 8](gp-da-particle).

**Ne … ne (de)** is **neither … nor**, and in standard Turkish the verb stays **positive**, because *ne* already does the negating: *Ne Ali geldi ne Ayşe* (Neither Ali nor Ayşe came). A negative verb (*Ne Ali gelmedi…*) is heard in speech but counts as a mistake in writing.

**Ya … ya (da)** offers two choices, one of which will happen ([B2 unit 8](gp-ya-particle)). **İster … ister** says the choice doesn't matter, **whether … or**, often with an imperative or a third-person imperative: *İster inan ister inanma* (Believe it or not), *İster gelsin ister gelmesin, biz başlıyoruz* (Whether he comes or not, we're starting). **Gerek … gerek(se)** is the formal **both … and**, mostly written.

items.tr: Hem güldük hem ağladık.
items.en: We laughed and cried.

items.tr: Ne Ali geldi ne Ayşe.
items.en: Neither Ali nor Ayşe came.

items.tr: Ne aradı ne bir mesaj attı.
items.en: He neither called nor sent a message.

items.tr: İster inan ister inanma, konser bedavaydı.
items.en: Believe it or not, the concert was free.

items.tr: Gerek öğrenciler gerekse öğretmenler konsere katıldı.
items.en: Both students and teachers attended the concert.

blocks.text: With *ne … ne*, keep the verb positive: *Ne çay ne kahve içerim*, not *içmem*.
French **ni … ni** needs a **ne** on the verb as well (**Je ne bois ni thé ni café**). Turkish *ne … ne* doesn't: the verb is simply positive.

summary: `-DIğI sürece` (formal `-DIğI müddetçe`) is **as long as**: *Çalıştığın sürece başarırsın*. With nouns and *var*: *olduğu sürece*.
`-mAdIkçA` is **unless**, with no possessive: *Sen söylemedikçe kimse bilmez*. `-mAdIğI sürece` and the plain `-mAzsA` say much the same.
In rules and notices: `-DIğI takdirde`, noun + *hâlinde* and `-mAsI hâlinde`. For something less likely: `-(y)AcAk olursa`, with the person on *olursa*.
Time clauses with `-DIk` + possessive: *geldiğin zaman* (when), *geldiği an* (the moment), *geldiği sırada* (just as), *geldiğinden beri* (since); and *gelene kadar* (until), with no possessive.
Paired words: *hem … hem* (both … and), *ne … ne* (neither … nor, with a positive verb), *ya … ya* (either … or), *ister … ister* (whether … or), *gerek … gerekse* (formal both … and).
